title: How to Reduce Taxes in Retirement Using Withdrawal Sequencing
description: The 'Tax Bracket Management' strategy to make your portfolio last longer.
content:
You spent 40 years diversifying your investments (Stocks vs. Bonds). Now, you must diversify your tax strategy. Retirement withdrawals are not all taxed the same. Money from a Traditional IRA is taxed at up to 37%. Money from a Brokerage account is taxed at 0-20%. Money from a Roth is taxed at 0%. By strategically pulling from specific accounts in specific amounts, you can manipulate your Adjusted Gross Income (AGI) to pay the absolute minimum tax legally allowed. This guide explains the 'Proportional Withdrawal' vs. 'Sequential Withdrawal' debate.

Key Takeaways

  • The Standard Deduction Fill: Every year, the first ~$29,200 (married) of income is tax-free. Always pull this amount from your Traditional IRA first to use up this '0% bracket'.
  • The Capital Gains Fill: Long-term capital gains are taxed at 0% if your income is under ~$94k (married). Fill this bucket next by selling taxable brokerage assets.
  • The Roth Top-Off: If you need more cash but don't want to jump into a higher tax bracket, pull the rest from your Roth IRA. It generates cash flow without generating taxable income.
  • RMD Defense: Spending down Traditional IRAs early (before age 73) can reduce your RMDs later, preventing a 'Tax Torpedo' in your 80s.

Why It Matters (US Context)

Social Security taxation is complex. If your 'Combined Income' is too high, 85% of your Social Security becomes taxable. Strategic withdrawal sequencing keeps your reported income low, preserving the tax-free status of your Social Security benefits.

The Withdrawal Waterfall

Example: A couple needs $100,000 cash to live.

Bucket 1: Traditional IRA (The Base)

Withdraw: $29,200.
Tax: $0 (Standard Deduction).
Result: You have $29k cash and $0 taxable income.

Bucket 2: Taxable Brokerage (The 0% Zone)

Withdraw: $50,000 (Assumes $25k basis, $25k gain).
Taxable Gain: $25,000.
Total Taxable Income: $25,000.
Tax Rate: 0% (You are under the $94k limit).
Result: You now have $79k cash and paid $0 federal tax.

Bucket 3: Roth IRA (The Gap Closer)

Withdraw: $21,000.
Tax: $0 (Always).
Final Result: You spent $100,000 and paid $0 to the IRS.

Which Method is Best?

  1. Conventional Wisdom (Sequential): Spend Taxable first, then Traditional, then Roth. This lets the tax-advantaged money grow longest. Downside: Giant tax bills in your 70s due to RMDs.
  2. Modern Wisdom (Proportional): Spend a little from all three every year to smooth out the tax bill. Keep your tax bracket steady at 12% or 22% throughout retirement.
  3. The 'Bracket Topping' Strategy: Fill the 12% bracket with Traditional withdrawals (or Roth Conversions). Stop there. Use Roth/Cash for any lifestyle needs above that limit.

Frequently Asked Questions

Do I need a CPA?

Yes, or good software (like NewRetirement or Pralana). The interaction between Social Security taxation, ACA subsidies, and capital gains brackets is hard to do in a spreadsheet.

What about state taxes?

Some states exempt retirement income (PA, MS). Others tax it fully. Your withdrawal strategy might change if you plan to move states later.

Does spending Roth money first make sense?

Rarely. Roth is your most valuable asset (tax-free growth). Usually, you want to preserve it as long as possible for late-life healthcare or inheritance.
